papers.title: Certified pandigital approximations of $\pi$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ and $e$
papers.abstract: In 2004 Erich Friedman asked for the best approximations of $\pi$, $e$, the Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ and Feigenbaum's constant $\delta$ that use each of the digits $1,\dots,n$ exactly once, with addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, exponentiation, parentheses and the decimal point. We determine the optimal expressions for $\pi$, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ for every $n \le 9$, with the digits in any order and in increasing order, and for $e$ when $n \le 6$. The optima are found by exhaustive search and certified by an independent algorithm that encloses every expression rigorously and decides each candidate with Arb and exact arithmetic; a second certified computation covers intermediate values of any size. Twenty-one entries improve the published records; for $\pi$ with the digits 1-9 the optimal error is $2.81\cdot 10^{-14}$. For $e$, whose records come from identities between power towers, we prove that Bamberger's formula is optimal within the natural family of such identities. All code and certificates are public.

papers.title: Fast Mixed-Precision Real Evaluation
papers.abstract: Evaluating real numbers to high precision is important in computational science, numerical computing, and in hardware and software design. Efficient algorithms exist for computing arithmetic operations and common elementary functions, but composing these primitives into larger expressions remains a challenge. The typical expression-evaluation algorithm computes all primitives in the expression to a uniform precision, doubling that precision until a sufficiently-accurate result is achieved. This is wasteful: usually only a few operations really need to be performed at high precision, and the bulk of the expression could be computed at a much lower, faster precision. However, no rigorous algorithm currently exists to compute these non-uniform precision assignments, nor to leverage non-uniform precision to reduce the number of primitive computations needed to evaluate an expression. We propose a new algorithm for deriving such rigorous precision assignments and reducing the number of primitive computations needed. This algorithm can leverage results computed at lower precisions to analytically determine a precision for each primitive that will result in a sufficiently-accurate evaluation. It can also use information from constant subexpressions, movability flags, and repeat flags to skip the computation of certain primitives, further reducing the time to evaluate real expressions. Our implementation, Reval, achieves an average speed-up of 3.97x compared to the widely-used Sollya tool, with the speed-up increasing to 9.26x on the most difficult inputs. A detailed evaluation shows that this speed-up results from both assigning lower precisions to the majority of primitives and from computing fewer primitives overall.
